Protein

 Home Biology
OurBigBook.com Words: 20k Articles: 492
A protein is a biological molecule made of one or more polypeptide chains: ordered amino acid residues joined by peptide bonds. Biological translation assembles a chain in the order specified by messenger RNA codons. Protein folding then brings parts of that chain into spatial relationships that support its function. See Cooper, The Cell: protein composition and structure. These processes can overlap in a biological cell; the sequence-to-shape explanation does not require waiting until biological translation finishes before any folding begins. See Cooper, The Cell: protein folding and processing.
The useful connection is from information to physical work. A protein's protein primary structure records an order; its protein tertiary structure can bring distant amino acid residues together at an active site. An enzyme uses such an arrangement to recognize a substrate and accelerate a chemical reaction. Other proteins serve as receptors, membrane transport proteins or structural material. For example, actin assembles into filaments whose mechanical properties can be described by biopolymer mechanics. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: protein function and binding.
Order matters beyond composition. Let A stand for alanine and M for methionine, and read from the N-terminus to the C-terminus. The illustrative strings AMAMAMAMAMAM and AAAAAAMMMMMM each contain exactly six A and six M amino acid residues. Each has 12−1=11 peptide bonds when made into one unbranched polypeptide chain. In the first string all eleven neighboring pairs have different letters; in the second only the pair at positions 6 and 7 does. A composition histogram therefore loses information about which amino acid residues are neighbors. Their arrangements can affect protein folding and function; these short invented strings neither specify a known functional protein nor establish what shape either would adopt.
Protein structure is a moving arrangement, not a permanently rigid outline. Substrate binding can change an enzyme's shape through induced fit, and a functional protein can include flexible regions. Sequence, surroundings and interacting molecules must therefore be considered together. See Alberts et al.: binding, conformational changes and protein function.

Simultaneous connection of separated DNA segments by a protein assembly. Intramolecular bridging produces a loop; intermolecular bridging connects distinct molecules.

DNA competition assay

Words: 71 Articles: 2
Protein–DNA interaction OurBigBook.com
A binding experiment challenging a labelled complex with unlabelled DNA. Specific and nonspecific competitors can distinguish sequence recognition from transfer of other DNA-bound components.

Nonspecific competitor DNA

Words: 24
DNA competition assay OurBigBook.com
DNA that lacks the selected recognition sequence but can accept nonspecific interactions or transferred histones. Its effect must be interpreted against controls for all components.

Specific competitor DNA

Words: 23
DNA competition assay OurBigBook.com
Unlabelled DNA containing recognition sites for the protein being tested. Competition can draw that protein away from labelled DNA without necessarily removing other proteins from the labelled assembly.

Ternary protein–DNA complex

Words: 25
Protein–DNA interaction OurBigBook.com
An assembly of DNA and two distinguishable protein components. A mobility shift alone does not establish composition; selective competition and component-specific detection can test which components remain.

An antibody is a protein that recognizes particular molecular targets through binding. Antibodies participate in immunity; laboratory assays such as Western blots exploit their selective binding to detect chosen proteins.
An IgG gives a concrete architecture: two immunoglobulin heavy chains and two immunoglobulin light chains, joined by disulfide bonds. Each arm ends in a paratope assembled from an antibody variable region of each kind of chain. The two paratopes recognize the same epitope in this conventional IgG; the flexible hinge allows different arm separations. The antibody constant regions form the remaining portions. This is an illustrative IgG, rather than the architecture of every antibody format. [ref]
Three questions must be kept separate. Antibody specificity asks which antigens are recognized. Antibody affinity describes one paratope–epitope interaction. Avidity describes the combined attachment when several contacts can cooperate. A selective antibody can have modest antibody affinity, and a monoclonal antibody can still show cross-reactivity. For an assay, the practical question is whether the observed readout identifies the intended antigen under the tested conditions; Western blot antibody specificity controls make that question concrete.

Gerald M. Edelman reduced IgG disulfide bonds and used dissociating chemical solutions, including 6molL−1 urea. The controls address distinct alternatives. Treatment-dependent separation supports chains joined in the starting protein; a matching gel electrophoresis position alone would not uniquely identify a chain. Agreement of peptide mapping adds an independent chemical comparison. Neither readout gives atomic coordinates, and this patient's preparation does not establish a common protein primary structure for all antibodies.
Reduction targets protein disulfide bonds, while protein denaturation weakens the folded assembly. Neither operation is the proteolysis that cuts peptide bonds. Words: 444
Fragment antigen-binding OurBigBook.com
Limited Papain digestion of IgG cuts each immunoglobulin heavy chain on the N-terminus side of the hinge crosslinks, releasing two Fab fragments and one Fc fragment.[ref]
A connectivity argument explains the three products. Treat each continuous backbone segment as a graph vertex, and retained interchain disulfide bonds as edges. After the two stipulated cuts, six backbone segments remain: two complete immunoglobulin light chains, two immunoglobulin heavy chain arm segments and two immunoglobulin heavy chain stem segments. Each light chain remains attached to its own arm segment, producing two separate Fab fragments. The two stem segments remain attached to each other, producing one Fc fragment. Thus six backbone segments form three connected components of a graph, not six independently released products. Removing crosslinks instead, while keeping each backbone intact, would leave four chain components in this simplified covalent-connectivity model.
For a constructed mixture, start with 5pmol of intact IgG and stipulate that 60% undergoes the complete two-cut event while the rest remains intact. Count amount of substance of each product:
nintact​=2pmol,nFab​=6pmol,nFc​=3pmol.
(1)
The total amount of separately connected products becomes 11pmol, although the starting amount was 5pmol. Each digested IgG replaces one connected assembly with three. The antibody binding site inventory is conserved in this model:
2nintact​+nFab​=(2⋅2+6)pmol=10pmol.
(2)
The factor two counts sites per intact IgG, not extra immunoglobulin light chains per Fab fragment. Fragment counts, backbone-segment counts and antibody binding site counts must be kept distinct. A real digest's retained binding would additionally depend on preservation of the paratopes.
The historical functional test was more subtle than asking whether a fragment still formed a visible precipitate. Rodney Robert Porter's earlier rabbit anti-ovalbumin preparation was digested with papain powder. The resulting fragment did not precipitate ovalbumin itself, but specifically inhibited ovalbumin precipitation with undigested antiserum. The intact-antiserum reaction supplied the positive comparison: failure to precipitate alone did not mean failure to recognize the antigen.[ref]
The inference is that binding and assembly of a precipitating network are different abilities. A one-site Fab fragment can occupy an epitope without providing the two-arm bridge available to intact IgG. The inhibition readout supports retained recognition under the tested conditions; it does not locate individual contacts or show that every papain-generated product binds. This is the conceptual benefit of fragmenting an antibody: one can ask which functions survive loss of a structural connection.

The last equality follows by substituting [AE]=[A]c/Kd​ into the occupied fraction and cancelling [A].

In the common SDS-PAGE version, protein denaturation and binding of an anionic surfactant reduce differences due to folded shape and intrinsic electric charge. Western blot transfer moves separated proteins out of the gel onto a Western blot membrane, using an electric field across the gel thickness. Maintaining close contact preserves the lane pattern. Contact gaps, incomplete removal from the gel and passage through the receiving sheet can change how much protein is retained.
The original 1979 experiment pressed a wetted, 0.45μm-pore nitrocellulose Western blot membrane against the gel between scouring pads and plastic pipette-tray grids, held by elastic bands. The urea-gel assembly faced the cathode in acidic solution, with 6V/cm applied for one hour; the SDS-PAGE variant reversed polarity and used a glycine/methanol buffer solution. Stained gel/blot pairs checked pattern preservation. Corresponding labelled ribosome protein spots from two gels were compared through radioactive decay readouts after combustion. The stained gel remaining after transfer supplied a removal check; a second receiving sheet revealed breakthrough on overloading. These tests supported recovery for the examined urea-gel proteins, within experimental variation, while the SDS-PAGE results showed unequal staining recovery. Preserved band positions therefore did not establish universal quantitative transfer. [ref]

Microsomal protein import experiment
Words: 510 Articles: 1
Cotranslational protein translocation OurBigBook.com
In 1975, Günter Blobel and Bernhard Dobberstein combined cell-free translation with dog-pancreas microsomes. Density-gradient centrifugation isolated the membranes; removal of resident ribosomes allowed reconstitution with rabbit-reticulocyte ribosome subunits. Added messenger RNA encoded an immunoglobulin light chain; globin provided a comparison. Products made with or without membranes were challenged with proteases and analyzed by SDS-PAGE and autoradiography. Membranes present during synthesis yielded processed, protected light chain; globin remained susceptible. Adding membranes after precursor synthesis failed to reproduce import. These comparisons support selective passage during synthesis in this preparation.[ref]
The companion paper specifies radioactive amino acid incorporation, ice-cold trypsin plus chymotrypsin treatment, a slab-gel electrophoresis apparatus and dried-gel exposure to X-ray film. Product-size analysis distinguishes a preserved full-size product from residual labeled fragments.[ref]
Protection was incomplete. The authors considered leaky vesicles, and warned that heat treatment could damage processing as well as ribosome attachment. Their experiments did not identify SRP or the Sec61 complex. Nor does failure of late membrane addition establish that all organelle protein import must occur during synthesis.[ref]
Protease protection assay
Words: 320
Microsomal protein import experiment OurBigBook.com
A protease protection assay asks whether a barrier prevents an added protease from reaching a protein. A membrane-disruption comparison tests whether protection depends on that barrier.
The membrane-disruption test was performed by David D. Sabatini and Günter Blobel in 1970. Rat-liver microsomes purified by sucrose centrifugation incorporated radioactive leucine during cell-free translation. Samples received cold trypsin and chymotrypsin, with or without membrane-solubilizing detergents. Electron microscopy checked vesicle preservation; size-exclusion chromatography separated protected fragment sizes. Large membrane-associated fragments lost protection after disruption, whereas small ribosome-protected fragments persisted. An exposed ribosome preparation remained digestible when mixed with microsomes, checking that membranes did not simply inhibit the proteases.[ref]
To read the qualitative diagram, first compare untreated aliquots: they establish that detectable cargo exists before digestion. Next compare external protease with intact versus disrupted membranes. Persistence only while the barrier remains intact supports enclosure, provided the exposed-cargo control confirms active protease in both chemical conditions. The detergent-only aliquot checks that disruption itself does not destroy recovery or detection. Adding membranes after synthesis tests a different alternative: capture of a completed product rather than entry during biological translation.
This is an argument from controlled accessibility. Binding predicts membrane association but generally leaves an exposed cargo digestible. Enclosure predicts protection that depends on membrane integrity. However, protein aggregation, intrinsic resistance to proteolysis, inactive protease or undetected small fragments can obscure this distinction. For a transmembrane protein, expect protection of the enclosed portion rather than necessarily the full chain. Combine fragment size, compartment controls and membrane topology; a protected signal alone does not uniquely specify the whole protein's location.

Protein primary structure

Words: 2k Articles: 12
Protein structure OurBigBook.com
The protein primary structure specifies the ordered amino acid residues of each polypeptide chain, joined through peptide bonds. A chain is conventionally written from its N-terminus to its C-terminus. In the broader chemical sense, a complete protein primary structure also specifies covalent bond crosslinks between chain positions, including protein disulfide bonds; a bare sequence string leaves that information unstated. This describes chemical connectivity rather than the spatial arrangement of protein tertiary structure or protein quaternary structure. See IUPAC Gold Book: primary structure, sequence and chain crosslinking and IUPAC-IUB, 3AA-16: writing residue sequences from the amino end. Some conventions reserve protein primary structure for sequence alone and call the complete chemical connectivity the covalent structure; the distinction should be stated when comparing descriptions. See IUPAC-IUB polypeptide-conformation recommendations, section 6.1: the narrower sequence-only convention.
In this toy example M denotes methionine, A alanine and G glycine. Both polypeptide chains have six amino acid residues, five peptide bonds, an M at the N-terminus and a G at the C-terminus. Their amino acid composition is identical, yet position 2 is A in MAGAMG and M in MMAAGG. There are 6!/(2!2!2!)=90 distinct orders with these counts, a multinomial coefficient. Even fixing those two end residues leaves 4!/(1!2!1!)=12 orders. The counts constrain the answer without determining it.
For multiple polypeptide chains, record each sequence separately and specify any protein disulfide bonds between cysteine positions. Mature insulin, for example, has an A chain of 21 amino acid residues and a B chain of 30 amino acid residues. Their combined 51 residues give (21−1)+(30−1)=49 peptide bonds, rather than the 50 of one unbroken 51-residue chain. See Cooper, The Cell: insulin's two chains and cysteine crosslinks, figure 2.16. A protein disulfide bond joins side groups; it does not concatenate the C-terminus of one chain with the N-terminus of another. The three insulin protein disulfide bonds connect A6 to A11 within the A chain, and A7 to B7 and A20 to B19 between chains. Positions are numbered from each chain's N-terminus. See Replacement of the interchain disulfide bridge-forming amino acids A7 and B7 by glutamate impairs the structure and activity of insulin: native disulfide positions.
Why keep this information? Protein primary structure lets us distinguish changes of chemical identity from changes of shape, and compare corresponding positions between proteins. Protein folding can bring distant amino acid residues together at a protein binding site while preserving their sequence. The attractive idea is that a readable linear record can constrain a complicated three-dimensional object; it is not, by itself, a guarantee of a unique fold in every environment. See protein folding and the ribonuclease A refolding experiment. Merely bending an intact chain preserves its protein primary structure; hydrolysis of a peptide bond, or changing which positions a protein disulfide bond connects, changes its chemical connectivity.

Sanger's insulin sequencing experiment

Words: 513
Protein primary structure OurBigBook.com
The motivating question was experimental: how could one recover the order in a protein when breaking all its peptide bonds destroys that order? Frederick Sanger and colleagues used complementary tests on portions of insulin. The following is an explanation of their evidence, not a laboratory recipe.
First, mark ends before destroying the chains. Sanger used the colored reagent fluorodinitrobenzene, abbreviated FDNB, to label free amino groups. After acid hydrolysis, the attached label remained on the end-residue products. Separating these derivatives by their different movement through solvents and comparing them with reference derivatives made the labels readable. The N-terminus products identified glycine and phenylalanine. Sanger emphasized that finding a stable label and a way to separate its products were both essential. See Sanger, Citation Classic (1985), discussing The free amino groups of insulin (1945). FDNB also labels suitable free amino groups on amino acid side chains, so a labeled product is not automatically an N-terminus product. See Sanger, The Chemistry of Insulin, Nobel lecture (1958), pp. 546–547.
Next, separate chains and preserve local order. Oxidation with performic acid broke the protein disulfide bonds, allowing A and B chains to be isolated. Partial hydrolysis and enzyme treatments produced fragments; these were separated and their composition and local sequences characterized. Overlaps between different fragment sets linked smaller sequences into longer ones. Many more fragments than minimally necessary were checked for consistency. See Sanger's authored Nobel lecture, pp. 547–552: chain separation, fragment analysis and sequence reconstruction.
The toy fragments make the logic visible. Suppose one cut pattern yields MAG and AMG, and another yields MA, GA and MG. The first set alone permits MAGAMG or AMGMAG. The fragment GA in the second set crosses the MAG–AMG boundary in MAGAMG; it does not occur in AMGMAG. Among concatenations of the first set, therefore, the second set selects MAGAMG. This example assumes intact, correctly identified fragments from one homogeneous chain and known fragment membership in each cut pattern. Repeated stretches, missing fragments or sample mixtures can leave ambiguities; the picture illustrates inference from overlaps, not a universal guarantee of reconstruction.
Finally, determine the protein disulfide bonds separately. Oxidation used to separate whole chains erases their original connections. Sanger and colleagues instead studied fragments still joined by protein disulfide bonds, then oxidized the isolated joined fragments to identify their component pieces and locate the connected chain regions. An important trap was rearrangement of disulfide bonds during treatment: products can acquire connections absent from the starting protein. Their work therefore had to establish conditions that prevented rearrangement before interpreting a linked fragment as evidence. See Ryle and Sanger, A Disulphide Interchange Reaction, Nature 171, 1025–1026 (1953) and Sanger's Nobel lecture, pp. 553–554: preserving and identifying disulfide connections. The result was an experimentally constrained chemical structure rather than a composition list or a photograph of a fold.

Insulin

Words: 573 Articles: 3
Protein primary structure OurBigBook.com
Insulin is a protein hormone. Its mature form has two polypeptide chains; identifying their sequences and protein disulfide bonds provided the motivating example in Sanger's insulin sequencing experiment. See Cooper: insulin as a two-chain hormone, figure 2.16.
A meal illustrates the insulin side of blood glucose homeostasis: rising glucose stimulates beta cells in the pancreatic islets, and released insulin favors uptake and storage of fuel. Alpha cells produce glucagon, while delta cells produce somatostatin, which inhibits release of both insulin and glucagon. The pancreas therefore contains interacting sensor and secretory biological cells, rather than one undifferentiated source of hormones. [ref]
Insulin and glucagon are peptide hormones, built from amino acid residues joined by peptide bonds; glucose is a small carbohydrate molecule. A hormone changes signal transduction, not the identity of the fuel it regulates. Human mature insulin has 51 amino acid residues in two polypeptide chains. Beta cells process proinsulin to insulin and C-peptide, storing the products in secretory granules for exocytosis. Increased glucose metabolism raises the ATP-to-ADP ratio, tending to close ATP-sensitive potassium channels; depolarization and entry of calcium ions then trigger exocytosis. This is an important triggering pathway, with additional amplification and modulatory inputs.[ref]
Binding to the insulin receptor, a receptor tyrosine kinase, starts phosphorylation of the receptor and insulin receptor substrates. Recruitment of phosphoinositide 3-kinase and activation of Akt transmit a major metabolic branch. In skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, that branch helps move GLUT4 to the cell membrane, increasing glucose uptake by facilitated diffusion. GLUT4 is a membrane transport protein, not an insulin receptor. Insulin also favors glycogenesis in skeletal muscle and the liver, and inhibits lipolysis in adipose tissue. In the liver, suppression of glucose output involves enzyme regulation, gene expression, and indirect changes in substrate supply. Its relative direct and indirect contributions are more complex than a single Akt arrow. [ref]
Insulin is not a universal permission slip for glucose entry: red blood cells and much of the nervous system use uptake mechanisms that are not acutely dependent on insulin. Nor does the liver use the same GLUT4 switch as skeletal muscle. This is why reduced insulin action can change blood glucose dramatically without stopping all glucose uptake. [ref]
Diabetes can disrupt production, response, and counterregulation. Type 1 diabetes usually involves destruction of beta cells and severe loss of endogenous insulin; type 2 diabetes combines insulin resistance with insufficient beta cell compensation. High circulating insulin can therefore coexist with impaired insulin action. Inappropriate glucagon release can add to excessive liver glucose output, and the response to low blood glucose can also be impaired: "more glucagon" is not a complete description of diabetes. These distinctions explain mechanisms, rather than prescribe treatment. [ref] [ref]

Glucose clamp technique
Words: 169
Insulin OurBigBook.com
Glucose clamp technique: a method for quantifying insulin secretion and resistance. by R. A. DeFronzo and others separates two questions. In a hyperglycemic clamp, variable glucose infusion holds blood glucose above baseline while sampled insulin reports the response. The 1979 article's abstract reports an early release burst followed by a slower rise. In a euglycemic insulin clamp, infused insulin is held elevated and variable glucose infusion holds blood glucose at baseline. Frequent blood sampling, a glucose analyzer, and controlled infusion apparatus make the imposed concentration a maintained condition rather than an uncontrolled consequence. [ref][ref]
The maintained glucose level controls an important confounder: a change in blood glucose would itself change uptake and hormone release. At a steady state, conservation of mass gives uptake equal to infused supply plus endogenous production, after accounting for losses. Consequently, infusion alone estimates uptake only if endogenous production is negligible and the other balance assumptions hold. Labelled glucose measurements can estimate residual endogenous production; matching infused insulin across comparisons matters. Whole-body uptake cannot by itself identify the responding tissue, and plasma insulin reflects both release and removal. This interpretation uses the accessible 1979 abstract and the later authored methods chapter; the original article's full methods were not available for inspection.[ref]

Protein structure OurBigBook.com
Protein secondary structure consists of recurring local arrangements of the protein backbone, notably the alpha helix and beta sheet. Backbone hydrogen bonds help stabilize these patterns. A beta sheet can bring together stretches far apart in the protein primary structure; local refers to the pattern of backbone geometry, not necessarily neighboring sequence positions. See Alberts et al.: alpha helices, beta sheets and backbone interactions.

Alpha helix (α)

Words: 86
Protein secondary structure OurBigBook.com
An alpha helix is a coiled protein secondary structure with a repeated pattern of backbone hydrogen bonds. In the standard pattern, the backbone group of amino acid residue i bonds to that of residue i+4: for example, positions 2 and 6. This is an additional spatial interaction, not a replacement peptide bond between those positions. Pauling, Corey and Branson proposed the helical arrangement in their 1951 paper by reasoning from the geometry of small molecules. See Pauling, Corey and Branson, The Structure of Proteins: Two Hydrogen-Bonded Helical Configurations of the Polypeptide Chain, PNAS 37, 205–211 (1951).

Beta sheet (β)

Words: 692 Articles: 3
Protein secondary structure OurBigBook.com
A beta sheet consists of extended stretches of protein backbone lying alongside one another, joined by backbone hydrogen bonds. The stretches can belong to different portions of the same polypeptide chain or to different chains.
Each extended stretch is a beta strand. Neighboring beta strands pack side by side, with repeated backbone hydrogen bonds between their backbone C=O and N−H groups: the oxygen is a hydrogen bond acceptor, and the backbone nitrogen with its attached hydrogen provides a hydrogen bond donor. These are interactions of the shared protein backbone, not merely contacts between amino acid side chains. Unlike an alpha helix, a beta sheet joins adjacent extended stretches rather than coiling one stretch around an axis. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 3.4: backbone groups in secondary structure.
Read each beta strand in the sequence direction from the N-terminus toward the C-terminus, even when it is an internal part of a longer polypeptide chain. In a parallel beta sheet, neighboring beta strands run in the same N→C direction; in an antiparallel beta sheet, they run in opposite N→C directions. A three-strand example can therefore have arrows right–right–right or right–left–right. A beta sheet can also mix the two arrangements. Direction does not identify chain membership: a single polypeptide chain can fold back to supply several beta strands, and different polypeptide chains can contribute to one beta sheet. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: beta-sheet strand arrangements.
The pleated appearance comes from the geometry of the protein backbone. Successive amino acid residues carry amino acid side chains on alternating faces of an ideal beta strand, conventionally drawn above and below the sheet. The attachment positions are the amino acid alpha carbons. Thus a six-position cartoon has groups 1, 3 and 5 on one face and 2, 4 and 6 on the other. This alternation is a spatial pattern, not a rule that alternating positions must contain identical amino acids. See Clark, Douglas and Choi: side chains above and below the pleats.
Real beta sheets commonly twist and curve; pleating does not make them perfectly flat plates. Which beta strands are neighbors, how connecting regions join them, and how their faces pack are features of the three-dimensional protein structure. An alternating pattern in the protein primary structure alone neither establishes a beta sheet nor specifies a unique fold independently of surroundings and interacting molecules. See Breda et al., Protein Structure, Modelling and Applications: extended strands, sheet twist and three-dimensional organization and protein folding.
Why this arrangement is useful: repeated backbone hydrogen bonds organize extended chain regions into a framework that can contribute to the interior of a folded protein. Amino acid side chains and connecting loops give that framework chemical variety and can shape a protein binding site for a ligand. Its attractive feature is the combination of a reusable backbone pattern with variable exposed groups: similar beta sheets can support different recognition surfaces. See Alberts et al.: beta-sheet cores and loops that form binding sites.
Historically, Linus Pauling and Robert B. Corey published The Pleated Sheet, a New Layer Configuration of Polypeptide Chains in PNAS 37, 251–256 (1951). They reasoned from peptide bond geometry and possible backbone hydrogen bonds, proposing an idealized layer rather than measuring every modern beta sheet. Their initial model should not be identified with all present-day beta sheet geometries; they published further pleated-sheet configurations later in 1951. See Pauling and Corey: original 1951 paper and scan, [ref], and Pauling and Corey, Configurations of Polypeptide Chains With Favored Orientations Around Single Bonds: Two New Pleated Sheets, PNAS 37, 729–740 (1951).

Protein secondary structure OurBigBook.com
A backbone hydrogen bond is a hydrogen bond involving groups of the protein backbone, typically a backbone oxygen chemical atom and a hydrogen chemical atom already joined by a covalent bond to backbone nitrogen. It can connect positions that are not adjacent along the polypeptide chain. The peptide bonds still determine which amino acid residues are consecutive. See the original structural argument cited under alpha helix.

Protein structure OurBigBook.com
The protein tertiary structure is the overall spatial arrangement of one polypeptide chain. It includes how its protein secondary structures and intervening regions fit together. For example, the schematic under protein places positions 4 and 9 near each other despite their separation in protein primary structure. Such cooperation can help construct an active site; sequence distance and spatial separation answer different questions. Hydrophobicity, backbone hydrogen bonds and other interactions help stabilize folds, and some proteins additionally contain protein disulfide bonds. See Cooper: tertiary structure and interactions between chain regions.

A protein binding site is a region of a protein structure that interacts with a ligand. Its arrangement of amino acid residues helps determine recognition; connecting loops supported by a beta sheet can contribute to it. An enzyme's active site binds a substrate and accelerates a chemical reaction. See Alberts et al.: protein binding sites and active sites.

A protein disulfide bond is a disulfide bond linking two sulfur chemical atoms carried by suitable amino acid residues. It can connect distant portions of a polypeptide chain or different chains. See Cooper: sulfur-containing residues and disulfide crosslinks. The four internal protein disulfide bonds of ribonuclease A are central to the ribonuclease A refolding experiment; breaking these crosslinks need not break the peptide bonds along its protein backbone.

Protein structure OurBigBook.com
The protein quaternary structure is the arrangement of multiple polypeptide chains in a functional assembly. A single-chain protein has protein tertiary structure without requiring protein quaternary structure. For an exact bookkeeping example, two intact model chains of twelve amino acid residues each contain 2×12=24 residues and 2×11=22 peptide bonds. Assembly alone adds no peptide bond joining their ends. Stable functional assembly should also be distinguished from protein aggregation. See Alberts et al.: proteins as assemblies of polypeptide subunits.

Protein folding

Words: 477 Articles: 6
Protein OurBigBook.com
Protein folding is the process by which a polypeptide chain acquires an organized spatial arrangement. The interactions of its amino acid residues with one another and the surroundings favor some arrangements over others. Protein folding can bring chemically useful groups together at an active site without changing their order along the protein backbone. Its importance is practical: knowing a sequence alone does not tell us whether a sample has the structure needed for function. See Cooper: acquiring functional protein structure.
The ribonuclease A refolding experiment showed that an isolated protein could recover its native properties without a pre-existing folded template under suitable laboratory conditions. Anfinsen interpreted this through a thermodynamic hypothesis: the native arrangement minimizes the whole system's Gibbs free energy in the appropriate environment. His Nobel lecture was delivered on 11 December 1972 and published in Science in 1973. The specified environment is part of the claim, not a disposable qualification. See Anfinsen, Principles that Govern the Folding of Protein Chains, Science 181, 223–230 (1973): Nobel lecture, especially p. 223.
This does not imply that every protein rapidly folds unaided. Molecular chaperones can assist protein folding and reduce protein aggregation; required partners, surroundings and time still matter. Goloubinoff and colleagues' 1989 reconstitution experiments demonstrated assistance from two molecular chaperones and ATP in recovering an active enzyme from unfolded chains. This is experimental evidence that assistance can matter even when the chains already have their specified sequences. See Goloubinoff, Christeller, Gatenby and Lorimer, 1989: chaperone-assisted reconstitution of an active enzyme.

Folding while a chain is being synthesized. Changes in elongation timing can affect the resulting folded and functional fraction.

An inclusion body in recombinant protein production is an insoluble aggregate-rich fraction containing the expressed material. Abundance does not demonstrate native folding; any recovered refolded product needs independent identity, assembly and activity checks.

A representation of which pairs of residues in a protein are in contact. In a lattice model, nonconsecutive residues may count as contacting when their lattice sites are adjacent. Several geometric foldings can have the same contact map, making it useful for compressing an enumeration of self-avoiding walks.

Protein folding OurBigBook.com
A folding funnel is a schematic energy landscape in which increasingly native-like protein conformations tend to have lower free energy, while the many unfolded conformations occupy a broad region. Roughness represents barriers and possible kinetic traps. The funnel is an organizing description, not a claim that every protein follows one unique geometrical trajectory or possesses a rigid isolated native state.

Protein folding OurBigBook.com
Conformational entropy measures the multiplicity of molecular conformations compatible with specified macroscopic constraints. For equally weighted accessible conformations it is kB​lnΩ; for probabilities pi​, it is −kB​∑i​pi​lnpi​. A folded protein generally has less chain conformational entropy than its unfolded ensemble, but folding can still lower total Gibbs free energy when solvent and interaction contributions are included.

A molecular chaperone is a protein that assists other proteins in reaching or maintaining useful arrangements, for example by limiting unwanted association during protein folding. Assistance does not rewrite the client's protein primary structure. In a crowded cytoplasm, reducing protein aggregation can make successful protein folding more reliable. See Cooper: molecular chaperones and folding assistance.

Words: 267 Articles: 1
Protein OurBigBook.com
Protein denaturation is the loss of a protein's native spatial organization, often with loss of biological function. Changes in temperature, pH or surroundings can disrupt protein secondary structure, protein tertiary structure or protein quaternary structure. Protein denaturation ordinarily preserves the peptide bonds and protein primary structure; it is different from cutting the chain. Recovery by protein folding is possible in some cases, but removing the denaturing conditions does not guarantee that every protein recovers. See Clark, Douglas and Choi: denaturation, environmental conditions and loss of function.
In the diagram, unfolding preserves all eleven peptide bonds. Cleaving the connection between positions 6 and 7 leaves two six-residue fragments: each contains five peptide bonds, so there are 5+5=10 in total. Simply cooling or otherwise restoring suitable conditions cannot recover the original chain by protein folding alone; the missing covalent bond would have to be remade. Conversely, protein aggregation can impede recovery without breaking any peptide bond. These distinctions explain why loss of function does not by itself reveal whether a protein unfolded, associated with other chains, or suffered chemical damage.

Protein aggregation is the association of proteins into clusters, often involving exposed regions of partly folded or unfolded polypeptide chains. It can prevent recovery of normal function while leaving the protein primary structures intact. It is distinct from both unfolding one chain and the functional assembly described by protein quaternary structure. See Cooper: partly folded chains, aggregation and chaperone protection.

Ribonuclease A

Protein OurBigBook.com
Ribonuclease A is an enzyme that catalyzes cleavage of RNA. The bovine pancreatic ribonuclease A studied by Anfinsen and colleagues has 124 amino acid residues and four internal protein disulfide bonds. It supplied a particularly informative test of the relationship between protein primary structure, protein folding and biological function: recovery could be measured through restored enzyme activity. See the primary sources under ribonuclease A refolding experiment.

Ribonuclease A refolding experiment

Words: 262
Ribonuclease A OurBigBook.com
Anfinsen, Haber, Sela and White's 1961 experiments began by treating bovine pancreatic ribonuclease A with mercaptoethanol in 8molL−1 urea. Urea promotes unfolding; mercaptoethanol breaks protein disulfide bonds. The peptide bonds along the chain remain intact. After separating the chain from those reagents, the authors allowed its reactive sulfur groups to form protein disulfide bonds in the presence of molecular oxygen, at pH 8.2 and temperature 23–24∘C. They examined protein concentrations of 0.1 and 2.0mgmL−1. Measurements showed recovery of native properties under these conditions; the isolated major component had normal activity toward both RNA and a synthetic substrate. See Anfinsen, Haber, Sela and White, The Kinetics of Formation of Native Ribonuclease during Oxidation of the Reduced Polypeptide Chain, PNAS 47, 1309–1314 (1961), pp. 1309–1311.
The observation supports the sufficiency of that intact sequence to recover native protein structure in the tested surroundings without a folded template. It does not establish that every protein refolds, that the original living biological cell needed no assistance, or that activity always returns immediately. Protein folding, forming protein disulfide bonds and recovering an active site are related processes rather than interchangeable measurements.
Anfinsen's lecture also discusses forming protein disulfide bonds while the chain remains in concentrated urea. This gave mostly inactive material; after removing urea, a small amount of mercaptoethanol permitted rearrangement toward the native form. As an exact combinatorial check, eight labeled reactive sulfur groups have 7×5×3×1=105 ways to be paired into four protein disulfide bonds: choose the partner of one group, then repeat with the unpaired groups. Only one pairing is the native one. Equal counting does not mean that all pairings are equally likely experimentally, nor that actual protein folding searches them uniformly. See Anfinsen's Nobel lecture, 1973 publication: scrambled ribonuclease and the 105 pairings, p. 223.

This illustrates why possessing the right amino acid residues is insufficient if their spatial arrangement is lost. See Alberts et al.: lysozyme as a worked example of protein binding and enzyme function.
A concrete structural example is Cheetham, Artymiuk and Phillips's 1992 study of hen egg-white lysozyme bound to a short carbohydrate that inhibits its action. The bound carbohydrate occupies part of the active site; it is not a reacting substrate in this complex. The study describes specific interactions and changes of shape accompanying binding. Thus a real binding site has chemical interactions and flexibility as well as a geometric outline. See Cheetham, Artymiuk and Phillips, 1992: structure of a lysozyme complex with bound inhibitor and RCSB PDB entry 1HEW: the authors' structure and bound three-unit carbohydrate. The diagrams above illustrate the idea; their twelve-residue strings are not lysozyme sequences or coordinates.

Receptor (biochemistry)

Words: 4k Articles: 41
Protein OurBigBook.com
A biochemical receptor is a protein that recognizes a signal and couples its detection to a biological effect. Its binding partner is a ligand; recognition depends on compatible shape and chemical interactions at a binding site within the protein structure. Specificity is selective recognition, not a guarantee that only one ligand can bind. Binding also need not activate the receptor: a competing ligand may occupy it while preventing activation by another ligand. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 4th edition: protein binding and specificity.
Compare a cell-surface receptor, accessible to an extracellular ligand, with an intracellular receptor, whose ligand must reach the interior. A cell-surface receptor can detect a hydrophilic ligand without transporting it through the cell membrane. In contrast, some membrane-permeable signals reach intracellular receptors that regulate gene expression. Location and downstream coupling are separate distinctions: an ionotropic receptor directly gates an ion channel, whereas a metabotropic receptor works through intracellular signal transduction. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 9.1: receptor locations and mechanisms.
Receptor binding occupancy quantifies recognition separately from response. A dissociation constant measures binding in a specified equilibrium model; it does not by itself predict the cellular effect. This separation is useful when comparing signals that bind equally well but produce different responses, or when interpreting a binding experiment alongside a functional measurement.

Ionotropic receptor

Words: 584 Articles: 2
Receptor (biochemistry) OurBigBook.com
An ionotropic receptor is a receptor in which binding of a ligand directly gates an ion channel within the same protein complex. The binding site detects the chemical signal; the pore supplies a path across the cell membrane. At a chemical synapse, a neurotransmitter therefore changes synaptic conductance without an obligatory intervening G protein or second messenger. [ref]
A familiar example is the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor of skeletal muscle: acetylcholine binding opens a pore passing cations, including sodium and potassium. The muscarinic acetylcholine receptor instead uses intracellular signal transduction; the same neurotransmitter can engage different mechanisms. Direct gating does not mean that an ionotropic receptor pumps ions: electrochemical gradients drive passage through the open ion channel. Nor does “ionotropic” specify excitation. The reversal potential, initial membrane potential and other conductances determine whether the effect favors an action potential, causes hyperpolarization, or supplies shunting inhibition. [ref]
A concrete electrical approximation separates opening from drive. Let N identical ion channels each have open-channel electrical conductance γ and opening probability p(t). At fixed membrane potential V, with common reversal potential Erev​, the expected value of inward-positive electric current is
Iin​(t)=Nγp(t)(Erev​−V).
(7)
For stipulated values N=100, γ=20pS, p=0.2, V=−60mV and Erev​=0, the mean open count is 20, the population electrical conductance is 0.4nS and Iin​=24pA. One open ion channel carries 1.2pA. These are illustrative values, not measurements. At V=Erev​, the net electric current vanishes despite open ion channels; neither binding nor opening alone determines the readout. The approximation omits changes in ion concentrations and voltage-dependent open-channel electrical conductance.
A motivating experiment made the elementary electrical events visible. As Bert Sakmann recounts, chronically denervated frog muscle fibers had acetylcholine-sensitive receptors spread beyond the original nerve contact. Mild enzyme treatment exposed the cell membrane; a polished glass pipette sealed over a small patch to reduce background noise. Two intracellular electrodes held the local membrane potential through voltage clamp, while the patch pipette recorded tiny electric currents. Applying suberyldicholine, a ligand that activates the acetylcholine receptor and prolongs openings, revealed abrupt, approximately rectangular current events. Their amplitudes agreed reasonably with estimates from whole-membrane current fluctuations. This established discrete opening and closing events; it did not make every ligand response instantaneous. Background noise and finite recording bandwidth concealed sufficiently small or brief events.[ref]
Recording an intact membrane patch alone does not exclude intracellular relays. Tank, Huganir, Greengard and Webb supplied a complementary isolation test in 1983: they purified nicotinic acetylcholine receptors from an electric ray's electric organ, incorporated them into artificial lipid membranes, and fused small vesicles into larger vesicles by freezing and thawing. Sealed glass-pipette recordings from isolated membrane patches resolved functional ion channels with properties resembling those in muscle. Removing the intact cytoplasm and its signaling machinery supports the sufficiency of the receptor complex for channel function; an artificial lipid environment still cannot reproduce every native regulatory interaction.[ref]
Direct gating supports millisecond communication at many chemical synapses. Response duration also depends on neurotransmitter clearance, binding and channel-state transitions. Continued ligand exposure can prolong activity. Classify an ionotropic receptor by its direct connection between recognition and pore gating, rather than a universal duration cutoff. [ref]

Metabotropic receptor

Words: 1k Articles: 14
Receptor (biochemistry) OurBigBook.com
A metabotropic receptor couples ligand recognition to intracellular signal transduction, which can regulate a separate ion channel, alter enzyme activity or change gene expression. In the usual neurotransmitter context, metabotropic receptors are G protein-coupled receptors: receptor activation is relayed by a G protein. There need not be a change in membrane potential at all. [ref]
Two routes should be distinguished. An activated G protein can regulate an ion channel locally at the cell membrane, without an obligatory diffusible second messenger. Alternatively, it can regulate an enzyme that changes the availability of a second messenger, such as cAMP or inositol trisphosphate. Downstream proteins then change channel opening, phosphorylation or other cellular activities. The receptor, G protein, second messenger and final target are distinct components; an activated G protein is a relay protein, rather than itself a small-molecule second messenger.[ref]
Do not turn this useful chemical synapse classification into the claim that every receptor is a GPCR, or that every indirect response must pass through a G protein. For example, the insulin receptor is an enzyme-linked cell-surface receptor whose intracellular catalytic activity initiates protein phosphorylation. Intracellular receptors supply another category. “Metabotropic” commonly names the GPCR branch in neuroscience; the broader idea of biochemical coupling does not make all non-channel receptors structurally identical. [ref]
Separating recognition from execution allows signal amplification and branching. A persistently activated receptor can activate several relay proteins; a regulated enzyme can produce many second messenger molecules. As an explicitly invented count example, suppose one activated receptor activates four relay proteins during one interval, and each relay activates a distinct enzyme that produces fifteen second messenger molecules during the next interval. With sufficient substrates and no loss, this gives 4×15=60 molecules. Those counts do not specify a physiological gain or response duration. A directly gated ion channel also passes many ions while open, so amplification is not an exclusive property of metabotropic receptors: always name the input and output being compared. [ref]
A particularly instructive electrophysiology experiment separated a chemical trigger from the ion channel carrying its eventual electric current. In 1987, Hirono, Ito and Sugiyama injected messenger RNA from rat brain into frog egg cells, then tested acquired responses to neurotensin and muscarinic acetylcholine stimulation. Under voltage clamp at −60mV, neurotensin elicited transient, oscillatory inward electric currents after a delay of several tens of seconds. This delay refers to that response and preparation. Reversal potential measurements implicated increased permeability to chloride anions, rather than a pore specific to the applied ligand. Both neurotensin and acetylcholine responses were inhibited by pertussis toxin, which interferes with susceptible G proteins, and by intracellular EGTA, which binds free calcium. Injecting inositol trisphosphate mimicked the responses; a large prior dose of inositol trisphosphate reduced subsequent responses to either extracellular signal. These interventions implicate a shared intracellular relay and calcium-dependent channel opening.[ref]
The informative comparison with the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor experiment is mechanistic: an extracellular ligand can produce an inward electric current either by directly gating the pore or by mobilizing an intracellular second messenger and stored calcium that activate another pore. Intracellular inositol trisphosphate bypasses reception, whereas EGTA tests the need for free calcium. However, neither inhibition nor mimicry alone identifies every molecular connection: a perturbation can affect several targets, and an injected mediator can activate a pathway without proving that it is the only natural route. The egg cell's endogenous machinery and the mixed messenger RNA preparation also limit extrapolation to an intact neuron. The experiment establishes functional coupling in its preparation, rather than the exact molecular composition or timing of every metabotropic receptor.
Even G protein-dependent channel regulation need not involve a lengthy second messenger cascade. Pfaffinger and colleagues reported in 1985 that acetylcholine-evoked potassium channel activation in embryonic chick atrial cells required intracellular GTP, a guanine-containing nucleotide, and was abolished by pertussis-toxin pretreatment. Changes in cyclic nucleotides, including cAMP, did not account for the channel response. The report discusses intrinsic activation delays of roughly 30–100ms, illustrating relatively rapid metabotropic receptor action. These observations support a G protein coupling step without cyclic-nucleotide second messengers; they do not by themselves exclude every possible intermediary or prove the specific subunit-channel interaction.[ref]
A small timing model makes the extra steps visible without inventing an experimental trace. Let u(t) jump from zero to one at t=0 and remain on. For a direct-gating model output d, one relay variable x, and its downstream output y, take zero initial conditions and
τd​dtdd​=u−d,τx​dtdx​=u−x,τy​dtdy​=x−y.
(8)
All outputs are normalized dimensionless variables; they are neither recorded electric currents nor fitted concentrations. With illustrative time constants τd​=2ms, τx​=20ms and τy​=100ms, their exponential function solutions for t≥0 are
d(t)=1−e−t/τd​,x(t)=1−e−t/τx​,y(t)=1−τy​−τx​τy​e−t/τy​−τx​e−t/τx​​.
(9)
Initially d′(0)=1/τd​, while y′(0)=0 because its relay must first build up. Both outputs eventually approach one. Equal normalized final values do not imply equal biological amplitudes or absence of signal amplification; normalization deliberately removes that question.
The model's useful feature is the delayed buildup created by sequential relaxation, not its arbitrary numbers. Actual kinetics also depend on ligand delivery, relay deactivation, neurotransmitter clearance and the final target. A local G protein route can act promptly, while an ionotropic receptor can remain active during continued exposure or feed a longer-lasting intracellular response. The beauty of metabotropic receptor coupling is its flexibility: the same recognition event can adjust electrical responsiveness and other cellular tasks through different targets. To classify an observed response, combine timing with molecular identity and controlled perturbations.

Epidermal growth factor receptor

Receptor tyrosine kinase OurBigBook.com
In an illustrative EGFR activation route, EGF stabilizes an associated pair of receptor chains. Asymmetric contact between their protein kinase protein domains activates one catalytic partner without requiring its activation-loop phosphorylation. Subsequent phosphorylation of cytoplasmic tails creates recruitment sites. Preassociated inactive EGFR populations can also occur: the cartoon's separated starting chains are not a universal initial condition.[ref]
Insulin receptor
Words: 110 Articles: 1
Receptor tyrosine kinase OurBigBook.com
The mature insulin receptor already contains two extracellular α chains and two membrane-spanning β chains, joined through protein disulfide bonds, before insulin binds. Insulin induces rearrangement of this (αβ)2​ assembly. Partner-mediated phosphorylation of the inhibitory activation loop permits increased protein kinase activity. Ligand-induced creation of a previously absent dimer is therefore an unsuitable universal explanation.[ref]
Insulin receptor substrate
Words: 47
Insulin receptor OurBigBook.com
An insulin receptor substrate is a docking protein phosphorylated by the activated insulin receptor. Its phosphotyrosine residues recruit downstream signaling proteins, including SH2 domain-containing components of phosphoinositide 3-kinase. This connects reception to the pathway described under insulin, rather than making the insulin receptor substrate another extracellular ligand.[ref]
Receptor phosphorylation assay
Words: 543 Articles: 1
Receptor tyrosine kinase OurBigBook.com
A receptor phosphorylation assay asks whether, and how much, a specified receptor is modified by phosphorylation under defined conditions. It is distinct from a binding assay for receptor binding occupancy, a test of protein kinase activity on a supplied substrate, and a test of downstream signal transduction. Those measurements answer related but different questions.
For a Western blot implementation, compare matched samples with ligand omitted or added, detect a specified phosphorylated epitope, and separately detect total receptor abundance. Preserve the sampled state by stopping further enzyme reactions during sample preparation; otherwise protein kinase or protein phosphatase activity after sampling can change the result. A general anti-phosphotyrosine residue antibody recognizes many modified proteins; a site-selective antibody gives a narrower readout, but still needs Western blot antibody specificity controls.
Reason through the controls before interpreting the difference. Loss of the proposed signal after receptor-specific gene deletion supports protein identity. Treatment with a protein phosphatase, alongside preservation of the total-receptor signal, tests phosphate-dependent recognition. Western blot loading controls and Western blot transfer controls address sample recovery; a usable detection range addresses Western blot response saturation. Lower signal after perturbing protein kinase activity supports dependence on that perturbation, but alternative targets and altered receptor abundance can complicate the inference. These are proposed assay comparisons, not outcomes attributed to the historical membrane experiment.
An original idealized measurement model explains the normalization. Let N be the retained number of receptor molecules, f the fraction carrying the selected modified epitope, and cp​,ct​>0 fixed detection gains. After subtracting their respective backgrounds, suppose the phosphorylated and total-receptor signals lie in a linear response range:
A=cp​Nf,B=ct​N,BA​=ct​cp​​f.
(10)
Dividing by total receptor cancels N under these assumptions. It differs from total-protein Western blot normalization, whose denominator includes many other proteins. For invented values cp​=ct​=1, samples with (N,f)=(100,0.2) and (200,0.2) give A=20 and 40, but both give A/B=0.2. Twice the phospho signal here means twice the retained receptor amount, with no change in fractional modification. Unequal recovery, changed epitope accessibility, nonzero uncorrected background or Western blot response saturation invalidates the cancellation. Unknown relative gains prevent reading an absolute modified fraction directly from the ratio.
Ligand-dependent membrane phosphorylation experiment
Words: 203
Receptor phosphorylation assay OurBigBook.com
A motivating experiment used isolated membranes from A-431 biological cells, which supplied abundant EGFR. Separate membrane aliquots were incubated at 0∘C with ATP carrying radioactive phosphorus in its terminal phosphate group, plus magnesium or manganese ions. Radioactivity in material recovered by chemical acid-induced precipitation supplied the readout. Adding EGF beforehand enhanced incorporation relative to the unstimulated preparation; this placed a ligand-dependent biochemical response in a cell-free membrane system.[ref]
The follow-up comparisons separated increased addition from suppressed removal: phosphate removal was rapid but unaffected by EGF, and anti-EGF antibody reversed activation by removing the ligand. These observations support reversible regulation of membrane-associated protein kinase activity.[ref] Total incorporation alone cannot identify which protein or amino acid residue received the label, prove intrinsic receptor catalysis, or predict an intact biological cell's response.
The same account records an instructive identification error: receptor phosphorylation was initially assigned to the wrong amino acid residue because released modified amino acids migrated together in the electrophoretic electric field. Reanalysis identified phosphotyrosine residues. Retained radioactivity is evidence about the assay's separation and detection, not unique chemical identity.[ref]
Reversible receptor phosphorylation model
Words: 171
Receptor tyrosine kinase OurBigBook.com
Protein kinase activity adds modification, while protein tyrosine phosphatase activity can remove it. An original one-site model shows why a receptor phosphorylation assay cannot determine either process from a single modified fraction. Let f(t)∈[0,1] be the fraction of a fixed receptor population carrying one selected phosphotyrosine residue. Stipulate constant effective first-order rate constants k+​,k−​>0, with ATP availability absorbed into k+​, and no receptor synthesis, degradation or trafficking:
dtdf​=k+​(1−f)−k−​f,f∗​=k+​+k−​k+​​,τ=k+​+k−​1​.
(11)
Here f∗​ is the steady state fraction and τ the time constant. The ordinary differential equation has the exponential function solution
f(t)=f∗​+(f(0)−f∗​)e−t/τ.
(12)
The balance equation and a single relaxation step give this result; it is an illustrative model, rather than a fit or a claim about every RTK.
With stipulated rate constants (k+​,k−​)=(2,1)min−1, f∗​=2/3 and τ=1/3min. Doubling both rate constants leaves f∗​=2/3 but changes τ to 1/6min. The balanced phosphate turnover per site,
J∗​=k+​(1−f∗​)=k−​f∗​=k+​+k−​k+​k−​​,
(13)
doubles from 2/3 to 4/3min−1. Identical steady state modification therefore permits different catalytic fluxes. Removing the addition term instead gives f(t)=f(0)e−k−​t; this illustrates why a perturbation that stops protein kinase activity can expose removal dynamics, subject to the model's unchanged-removal assumption. A maintained steady state with ongoing ATP consumption is not chemical equilibrium.

An intracellular receptor recognizes a ligand inside a biological cell, including in the cytoplasm or cell nucleus. Receptor binding occupancy (θ)

Words: 316
Receptor (biochemistry) OurBigBook.com
Receptor binding occupancy is the fraction of binding sites occupied by a ligand. Consider reversible, noncooperative binding at chemical equilibrium, with homogeneous independent sites: every site has the same binding properties, and binding at one site does not change binding at another. Let L denote free ligand, R an unoccupied receptor site and RL the bound complex. In this dilute concentration model,
L+R⇌RL,Kd​=[RL][L][R]​,RT​=[R]+[RL],θ=RT​[RL]​=Kd​+[L][L]​.
(14)
Square brackets denote concentrations; RT​ is the total site concentration. Here the dissociation constant Kd​ has concentration units. Use free ligand in excess so binding negligibly depletes it; only under that approximation may the supplied total ligand concentration substitute for [L]. See Analysis of Receptor–Ligand Interactions: equilibrium binding and saturation.
For an illustrative dissociation constant Kd​=10nM, where 1nM=10−9molL−1, free ligand concentrations 1, 10 and 100nM give θ=1/11≈0.091, θ=1/2=0.5 and θ=10/11≈0.909, respectively. At [L]=Kd​, exactly half the sites are occupied in this model. Raising [L] tenfold from 10 to 100nM raises occupancy from 50% to about 91%, rather than tenfold: the finite pool of sites causes saturation.
A short derivation uses the law of mass action: at chemical equilibrium, association balances dissociation, giving [RL]=[L][R]/Kd​. Substitute this into θ=[RL]/([R]+[RL]) and cancel [R] to obtain the displayed formula. The limiting values follow directly: zero free ligand gives zero occupancy, and increasing [L] far above Kd​ drives occupancy toward one.
Receptor binding occupancy is not automatically the fraction of maximal response. Signal amplification, differing effects of bound ligands, and downstream saturation can change the relationship. Consequently, [L]=Kd​ specifies half occupancy here; it does not universally specify either half-maximal or maximal cellular response. These numbers describe a toy binding model, not measured responses of every receptor. See Higham and Colquhoun, 2024: the affinity–efficacy problem.
